zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The returned transcription and review notes are separate scan-based work, not a reproduction of that index.

lines.note: Ruichoo is explained by tsukareta tori, a tired bird. The initial is R, not the OCR's B; the circumflex on the final vowel is retained.
The alternative Portuguese description is a weakened or debilitated bird; this short row completes Ruichô rather than beginning another entry.
Ruikon is exhaustion, explained by tsukare and kutabiruru. The Portuguese noun for fatigue is divided after canſa- at the right edge.
Completes canſaço and adds weakness as an equivalent. The final upright S is the written-register label, not part of the italic gloss.
Ruinen refers to years accumulating, as toshi kasanaru explains. Enlargement retains the unusual repeated re in acrecentarerenſe; this printed anomaly is not silently regularized.
The accumulating things are years; the alternative gloss is simply many years. This completes the preceding infinitival construction.
Ruikwa is glossed through onaji tagui no toga, wrongdoing of the same kind. The Portuguese prints Peccado with two c letters.

runs.text: da meſma eſpecie, ou peccado que da meſma

lines.note: The gloss first defines sin of the same species, then begins an alternative explanation of guilt falling in the same manner upon someone.

runs.text: maneira caye, ou carrega ſobre alguem como

lines.note: This continues the inherited or shared-guilt explanation: wrongdoing falls upon, or burdens, someone. The following row supplies its example.

runs.text: peccado dos pais ſobre os filhos, &c.

lines.note: The example is the parents' sin falling upon their children. It completes this Ruiqua entry and must not be joined to the separate fire sense below.

runs.text: Fogo que ſe pega na caſa vizinha.

lines.note: This homonymous ruikwa concerns a fire spreading from a neighboring house, not the wrongdoing defined in the preceding entry.
Ruikwa ni au is illustrated as being burned by a spreading fire. The historical vǒ spelling and its caron are preserved; Vt is italic apparatus.

runs.text: que ſe pegou na caſa do vezinho.

lines.note: The fire originated in the neighbor's house. The distinct printed forms vizinha above and vezinho here are retained rather than harmonized.
Ru ire is referred back to Ru. The visible gap in the headword is kept; the cross-reference is not silently expanded into an unattested definition.

runs.text: Inchaços, ou carouços q̃ nacem no peſ-

lines.note: Ruireqe denotes swellings or lumps around the neck. The scan has an initial R, and its final qe is preserved despite the following entry's similar spelling.
Coço completes peſcoço; the location is around the throat. The abbreviation tilde in gargãta is retained without supplying the omitted nasal letter.

runs.text: O chorar muito, ou por muito eſpa-

lines.note: Ruireki is prolonged or abundant weeping. Unlike the neighboring neck-swelling entry, this headword ends in qi; the Portuguese eſpa- continues below.
Completes eſpaço, here duration: weeping for a long time. The upright S marks written usage and is separated from the italic definition.
Ruitai is equated with daidai, successive generations or ages. The gloss's alternative wording continues onto the following physical row.
Many ages or generations completes the explanation of Ruitai. The short continuation is retained independently rather than merged into its headword row.
Ruitoku means accumulating merit, explained by toku wo kasanuru. The Portuguese infinitive acrecentar governs the noun on the next row.
The accumulated things are merits; the alternative definition is much merit. This is the completion of Ruitocu, not a separate example.
Ruiu is interpreted as namida no ame, a rain of tears. The visibly separated Rui v is preserved rather than joined in the canonical text.
The gloss adds abundant weeping. Rui v haregatashi supplies an example in which this rain of tears is difficult to clear or stop.

runs.text: O não poder reprimir, ou interromper as mui-

lines.note: The Portuguese explains inability to restrain or interrupt the tears. The negative belongs to the Japanese difficulty construction, and mui- continues below.
Tas completes muitas: the example concerns many tears. This short row closes the Ruiu entry before the distinct accumulated-ages sense.
Ruise denotes successive ages, explained by yo wo kasanuru and daidai. The Japanese particle remains attached in the printed Youo.
The Portuguese completes the definition as many ages or centuries. It reinforces the temporal sense of Ruixe rather than the tears of the previous entry.

runs.text: Embarcaçoẽs, ou nauios que vão de

lines.note: Ruisen denotes vessels traveling together. The headword begins with R, not OCR B; the tilde in Embarcaçoẽs is retained over its printed carrier.
De conſerua means sailing in company or convoy. This single-word row completes the fleet description above.
Ruisetsu is represented with the checked final t in Ruixet. The gloss specifies cords used to bind people, without expanding that final consonant.
Ruishin is kin or relatives, directly matched by Parentes. Its short definition is a complete independent entry.
Ruiyon means descendants or progeny. The Portuguese confirms a genealogical sense, distinct from the preceding general term for relatives.

runs.text: Boyãoſinho como pucaro pera meter o Cha

lines.note: Ruiza denotes a small pot, compared with a drinking vessel, for holding tea. The diminutive spelling Boyãoſinho is preserved as printed.
Moido specifies that the tea stored in this vessel is ground. This adjective completes the container's use, not a new entry.
Runin is an exile, equated with nagasarebito. The small comma after i is visible; the Portuguese describes the banished person.
Rukei is penal exile, equated with ruzai. The scan supports Ruzai rather than OCR Rozai, and the gloss specifies punishment for a crime.
Ruren is explained as wandering about, nagare ariku. The headword is abraded but readable; the Portuguese starts the expression for moving to and fro.
The visible grave in là completes de cà pera là, moving to and fro. A second sense begins: doing something while one's attention is elsewhere; fazen- continues below.

runs.text: do algũa couſa com o ſentido noutras partes co-

lines.note: Completes fazendo and describes an activity performed with the mind elsewhere. Com, not OCR dem, is supported by the remaining type and the syntax.
Mo completes como, comparing the absent-minded action to amusing or distracting oneself. The faint reflexive ending is retained as ſe, not fe.
Ruri names a blue precious stone. The general wording is retained without adding a more specific mineral identification to the transcription.
A separate Ruri entry describes a dark-blue bird. The headword is upright throughout; eſcuro corrects OCR eſruro without changing the printed bird-name spelling.
Ruri iro is a dark-blue color. The conspicuous printed spacing da zul is retained rather than normalized to d'azul or de azul.

Ruroo denotes exile, with an example meaning to wander in exile. The headword's final vowel is badly faded; Rurǒ is adopted from its residual outline and the clearer repeated form. No terminal hyphen is supplied after An.

runs.text: dar deſterrado ſem caſa, nem lugar certo.

lines.note: Dar completes Andar. The explanation is wandering in exile without a home or fixed place; the faded word deſterrado is kept intact rather than split as OCR suggested.
Ruroo no mi to naru means becoming an exile. The abraded initial is R, not X; the phrase's no mi to construction supports the retained word division mito.
Rusu is paired with todomari mamoru, staying to guard, while the first Portuguese gloss describes absence. Both aspects are preserved; the scan restores the missing letters in Ruſu and abſente.
The first sense is being away from home. Rusu wo suru introduces the complementary activity of remaining behind to look after the house.

runs.text: em caſa vigiãdo em abſencia dalguẽ. ¶

lines.note: The example means staying home on watch during someone's absence. The new Japanese example starts with Ru-, in upright type rather than part of the Portuguese.
Ru- plus ſu forms rusu; naru and dearu are alternative predicates for being absent. The lowercase l introduces the alternative and is not a Japanese syllable.
Rusumori is the person left to guard the house, explained as rusu no ban. The headword is wholly upright; guar continues below without an added hyphen.
Dando completes guardando, followed by watching the house as an equivalent. The row belongs to the caretaker definition, not to the next memory-related entry.
Rutsuu is explained as bringing something to mind, kokoro ni ukamuru. The printed vcamuru is preserved rather than changed to a modern expected verb form.

runs.text: ou ſaber bem de memoria as couſas.

lines.note: The second gloss is knowing things well by heart. It completes the memory sense of Rutçǔ and does not describe the following cycle of rebirth.
Ruten denotes circulation or revolution. The example begins shooji, birth and death: the damaged vowel has a caron, supporting Xǒji rather than OCR Xiji.
Shooji ni ruten suru is cycling through birth and death. The Portuguese begins the interpretation as being born again and dying.

runs.text: muitas vezes, como imaginão os gentios.

lines.note: The gloss completes the repeated-birth interpretation and attributes it to non-Christian belief in the compilers' terminology. This describes the historical source's viewpoint.

runs.text: O deſterrar, ou condenar ao deſterro

lines.note: Ruzai means banishing or sentencing to exile. Its verbal Portuguese explanation continues with the person subjected to that sentence.
Ruzai ni okonau illustrates imposing exile upon someone. The historical voconǒ and caron are retained; Idem refers back to the preceding definition.
Sa is an exhortative particle, illustrated below by an invitation to go. The decorated S belongs to this headword and spans six physical rows; OCR ornament fragments are not letters.
Sa mairoo is an exhortation to go, matching Portuguese Ea vamos. The caron marks the Japanese long vowel; the row remains beside the enlarged initial.
A separate sa means thus or in that way. Its explanation continues below; this ordinary-sized Sa is not part of the decorated initial above.
Sa nakuba is the conditional example, meaning unless it is so. The historical spelling naquua is retained instead of being modernized to the interpretive reading.

runs.text: Se aßi não for. Item, He

lines.note: The translation is 'unless it is so'. A grammatical description of the suffix sa begins with Item, He; there is no visible hyphen after He.

runs.text: particula que no cabo dalgũs no-

lines.note: The suffix is described as a particle added at the end of certain words. The decorated initial's lower ornament is excluded from the text; cabo replaces OCR cado.

runs.text: mes, ou preſentes de verbos faz fazer nomes

lines.note: Mes completes nomes; the explanation says the suffix forms nouns from certain names or present-tense verb forms. The source's grammatical categories are preserved without rewriting them.
The derived forms are substantives; migotosa illustrates the quality of being splendid or attractive. The printed ſuſtantiuos is not normalized by supplying b.
Completes the pleasing-appearance gloss for migotosa, then gives kaerusa as another formation, denoting returning or the return occasion.

runs.text: ou conjunção em que ſe hum torna.

lines.note: The second paraphrase of kaerusa is the occasion on which one returns. This completes the suffix discussion before the independent Saba entry.

runs.text: Salua que ſe toma do arroz cozido antes

lines.note: Saba is a portion taken from cooked rice before eating. The purpose of setting this portion aside follows on the next physical row.

runs.text: de o comer pera offerecer ao Fotoque. ¶

lines.note: The rice portion is offered to the Buddha before eating. Fotoque is a Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese sentence; Sa- begins the following example.
Sa- plus bauo gives saba wo toru, taking this offering portion. The Portuguese Salua sense is the reserved portion, not a modern ceremonial salute.
This separate saba entry names a fish and compares it to a shad-like fish. The historical Portuguese comparison is retained instead of substituting a modern species name.

runs.text: Couſa deßa laya, ou como eſ-

lines.note: Sabakari no describes something of that sort or degree. The Japanese modifier is printed as one headword, and the Portuguese demonstrative continues across the break.
This completes eſſa, 'that one', in the comparison above. The short continuation is not a new Japanese word or an omitted headword.
Sabaki, sabaku, sabaita means disentangling threads or hair here. The principal forms are preserved; the Portuguese list continues below.
Kami wo sabaku illustrates disentangling the hair of the head. The final De- is the beginning of the Portuguese translation on the next row.
Completes Deſempeçar and translates the hair-disentangling example. This closes the physical handling sense before the administrative homonym.
A second sabaku entry means managing affairs. The final infinitive is negocear, not OCR negoceas; the Portuguese object follows below.
The managed matters concern a household. The Japanese example begins with house and estate or revenue, iye and chigyoo, before continuing its object list.
Nando wo sabaku completes the example, managing such things. The Portuguese repeats taking care of and administering them, with admi- divided at the edge.
Completes adminiſtrar and identifies the house and income as its objects. This is the translation of the preceding Japanese management example.
The noun sabaki denotes administration or handling. Cou- begins the Portuguese noun for the things being managed on the next physical row.
Completes couſas and specifies household affairs. This ends the management noun before a separately defined cord or leash.

runs.text: Hum cordel, ou trela comque leuão

lines.note: A further sabaki entry denotes a cord or leash. Its use is described by the relative clause continuing on the next line.
The leash keeps dogs tied while they are taken hunting. The scan supports caẽs as one word; the following bottom-right fragment is a catchword, not another body row.
This abraded catchword anticipates the Saba- entry at the top of f427. It is page furniture, not a further sense of Sabaqi; the usable reading Saba. is retained.
